name: Geshiza
confidence_why: Honkasalo 2019's reference grammar of Eastern Geshiza gives final-syllable stress as the general rule, Vanderveen 2015 and Gates 2021 find the same second-syllable default in the sister variety Mazur Stau, and the initial stress that Tunzhi 2019 reports belongs to a different variety, Bra'go rTa'u, so the Geshiza reading has no first-hand opponent but rests on one hedged statement.

catalog_quote: [Honkasalo 2019: 203] Geshiza is best characterised as having a ‘pitch accent’ system that carries no function of distinguishing lexical meaning. ... Geshiza has no phonemic tone. ... Pitch patterns visible in the lexicon of the language cannot be completely predicted from either phonological or semantic factors. Geshiza pitch accent requires further research with several linguistically aware consultants. ... Some conclusions can nevertheless be drawn at the present stage. As a general rule, Geshiza stresses the ultimate syllable that is more prominent: rgæ.vvæ ‘stone’, a̯loŋ.bu.ttɕʰe ‘elephant’. When adding extra clarity to speech by pronouncing a word carefully in isolation, the ultimate syllable may be lengthened if it is open, i.e. lacking a final consonant. Two further first-hand grammars held by the project bear on the classification: Gates 2021 (Mazur Stau, EHESS PhD, sec. 2.5, pp. 116-122, p. 164) CONFIRMS — 'stress always goes to the higher pitched syllable', H-HF with second-syllable stress the isolation default, HL/first-syllable stress only in vocatives, negation prefix attracts stress; Tunzhi 2019 (Bra'go/BM rTa'u, La Trobe PhD, sec. 2.6, pp. 104-106) CONTRADICTS for that variety — 'Polysyllabic words exhibit a prominent stress on the first syllable when elicited in isolation', default H-L and H-L-L, stress morphologically contrastive (imperative prefix stressed). Jacques 2017 sketch is silent. new_statements.quote: From Vanderveen’s observation and my own, the HF syllable is the stressed syllable for H-HF, and the H syllable is stressed for HL. Since HF is higher than H for H-HF, be it ever so slightly, and H is obviously higher than L for HL, an important principle can be extracted: stress always goes to the higher pitched syllable. ... In summary, Vanderveen’s claims still hold up for pitch and stress for words given in isolation. ... For disyllables the basic pattern is H-HF, but for the vocative it is HL. ... we can say that for disyllabic words in isolated contexts H-HF and stress on the second syllable is the default.
new_statements.citation: Gates, Jesse P. 2021. A grammar of Mazur Stau. PhD thesis, EHESS, Paris (NNT 2021EHES0054), sec. 2.5.1 'Pitch and stress at the word level'.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.5.1, p. 122 (the text layerof the saved); supporting: sec. 2.5.2.2 vocative barytonesis; sec. 3.1.4.1 p. 164 stress displacement
new_statements.reading: A full reference grammar (2021, with pitch tracks) of Mazur Stau independently confirms Vanderveen 2015: word stress is pitch-realised, non-contrastive, and falls by default on the final (second) syllable of disyllables in isolation; first-syllable stress (HL) is a vocative phrase-level pattern for kinship terms and proper names, and grammatical prefixes such as perfective negation mæ- attract primary stress (rə-ˈmæ-ɕə-sə). This confirms the catalog's fixed and weight-blind ultimate-syllable coding for Mazur Stau and Geshiza. But Tunzhi 2019 (Bra'go rTa'u, same languoid) states the opposite default — prominent stress on the FIRST syllable of polysyllables, H-L / H-L-L — so the languoid's rule is variety-dependent and the record should note the Bra'go rTa'u initial-stress variety (or split it) rather than treat final stress as languoid-wide.

sources.citation: Gates, Jesse P. 2021. A grammar of Mazur Stau. PhD thesis, EHESS, Paris (NNT 2021EHES0054), dir. A. Vovin & G. Jacques.
sources.quote: [p. 122] Stress collocates with the syllable that has the higher pitch. In H-HF, the syllable with HF has the higher pitch and thus receives stress. ... In HL, H is the stressed syllable. However, we can say that for disyllabic words in isolated contexts H-HF and stress on the second syllable is the default. The examples of HL for kinship terms are the result of phrase level grammar (i.e., vocative expressions).
sources.note: Sec. 2.5 'Pitch, stress, and intonation' (pp. 116-122): suprasegmentals create no phonological distinctions; monosyllables HF (H a free variant); disyllables in isolation default H-HF with stress on the second syllable; HL with first-syllable stress only for vocatives (proper names, kinship terms) = 'barytonesis' (sec. 2.5.2.2); principle 'stress always goes to the higher pitched syllable' (p. 122). Stress displacement in prefixed verbs (rə-ˈɕə-sə vs rə-ˈmæ-ɕə-sə, p. 164) shows grammatical prefixes such as negation take primary stress. Confirms the catalog's word-final/second-syllable default…

sources.quote: Native-speaker grammar of the Brag-mda' (Zhangda) variety of rTa'u/Daofu: 'Polysyllabic words exhibit a prominent stress on the first syllable when elicited in isolation. BM rTa'u does not exhibit lexical contrasts based on pitch accent ... However, stress is contrastive on the morphological level'; 'In general, in disyllabic words the first syllable is stressed as in [ˈkʰɔʔ.χpə] 'body', and the same applies to prefixed words, where it is the prefix that receives stress as in [ˈtə=ɕə]'; default H-L for disyllables (/ˈmə.ko/ 'sky'), H-L-L for trisyllables (/ˈɕɔŋ.mbɑ.ʂtɑ/ 'hoopoe'); reduplicated

sources.citation: Vanderveen, A. Chantel. 2015. A Phonology of Stau. MA thesis, Trinity Western University.
sources.quote: [p. 151] Disyllabic words usually have stress on their second syllable; this is realized as a H-HF pitch pattern. Some complex disyllabic words, such as kinship terms and words ending with -rə, are realized with HL pitch; these have stress on the first syllable.
sources.note: Sec. 8.3 pp. 148-149 and ch. 9 p. 151: tentative fixed stress system; monosyllables HF; disyllables mostly H-HF = second-syllable stress; affixed HL disyllables (kinship terms, -rə words) first-syllable stress; greetings/leave-takings/times of day carry utterance-level intonation; words of 3+ syllables left for future research.

sources.citation: Tunzhi. 2019. Outline of Bra'go Variety of rTa'u (Horpa). PhD thesis, La Trobe University, Melbourne.
sources.quote: [p. 104] Polysyllabic words exhibit a prominent stress on the first syllable when elicited in isolation. BM rTa'u does not exhibit lexical contrasts based on pitch accent; that is, there are no minimal pairs of words that can be distinguished in terms of their pitch contour. This also applies to stress. However, stress is contrastive on the morphological level and it marks a variety of meanings. The BM rTa'u pitch-accent system can be simply described to have a High (H)-Low (L) sequence on syllables within a word, the accented syllable is the loudest and has the highest pitch. ... [p. 104-105] The default pattern for two syllable words is for the first syllable to be accentuated, with low pitch on the second syllable
sources.locator: sec. 2.6 'Pitch and stress', pp. 104-106; transcription conventions p. 47
sources.note: For the Bra'go (BM) rTa'u variety of Stau: polysyllabic words carry prominent stress on the FIRST syllable in isolation; pitch not contrastive; default H-L on disyllables (root+suffix and compounds included), H-L-L on trisyllables; reduplicated words accent the non-reduplicated element (ti.ti.ˈŋa 'small', ˈtsʰa.qɔ.qɔ 'warm'); stress is 'contrastive on the morphological level' (imperative prefix stressed, ˈtə=ɕə).
